head.html: Built and deployed for FRC Team 5417, FRCMOB is a full scouting platform: team workspaces and live multi-scout rooms, offline event packs, match predictions tested without hindsight, and a computer-vision breakdown that runs on the scout's own phone.

rows: Used by FRC Team 5417 at competition

head.html: FRCMOB is open source under the GNU AGPL v3. The public repository includes the web app, API, game configuration, deployment setup, documentation, and tests. Model weights, training data, match recordings, database contents, and credentials remain private.

blocks.html: Alliance selection is the highest-stakes decision a team makes at a competition, and it's usually made on thin evidence. The standard method is manual scouting: students in the stands watch a match and fill out a form. Six robots move at once for two and a half minutes. A scout tracks one of them, usually while also trying to count scoring cycles.

The data that comes back has predictable problems. Scouts miss things when the field gets crowded. Different people apply the same rating scale differently, so a "4 out of 5" from one scout doesn't mean what it means from another. Coverage is uneven, and the teams you most want data on are often the ones nobody was assigned to watch. And by the time you notice a gap, that match is over.

Video doesn't have those problems. It's complete, it's re-watchable, and it's the same every time you look at it. The obstacle is that nobody has the hours to watch it. FRCMOB started as an attempt to close that gap: process the footage automatically, then put a person in front of the result before it counts for anything. It grew into the rest of what a scouting team needs around that.

I began FRCMOB in February 2026 for my own team. Team 5417 has since used the platform at a real competition. Right now I'm working on running a full match breakdown on a real phone at an event, getting the native apps into the stores, and getting ready for the 2027 game.

blocks.text: The design constraint that shaped everything

blocks.html: A model that's right most of the time is not automatically useful here. If a strategy team can't tell which numbers to trust, a confident wrong answer is worse than no answer, because it gets acted on. So the system was built so that nothing produced by a model becomes accepted data on its own. Every automatic result carries a confidence value, and a human either approves it, corrects specific fields, or throws it out. The same rule ended up applying to my own numbers: if I can't measure it on data it hasn't seen, it doesn't ship.
Eight months, from a first commit to a platform. The spring was built around competitions, with fixes landing during events. The fall was about measuring it properly and keeping it running.

Everything spatial depends on one transform. A camera in the stands produces a foreshortened image where the far end of the field is compressed into a fraction of the frame. Strategy questions are about real positions. The homography is what connects the two, and if it's wrong every downstream metric is wrong with it.
Six stages take a scout's video to identified robot paths, and all six run on the phone. Select a stage to read what it does.

blocks.s: Why the AprilTag fallback exists

blocks.html: On paper, calibration is automatic: detect the fiducials, solve for the matrix, done. Testing on real footage showed the tags are frequently unresolvable at the distance and angle a phone in the stands actually films from. There are too few pixels on the tag to decode.

The fallback asks the scout to tap the four field corners once. That gives the same four correspondences without needing to read a single tag. It's a worse method in principle and the only one that works from row 20, which is why it's now the main path rather than the backup.

blocks.s: Reading team numbers off bumpers (tried, abandoned)

blocks.html: Tracking gives continuous paths, but not which team a path belongs to. The first answer was OCR on bumper numbers, with reads voted on across a whole track and matched against the six teams the schedule says are on the field. The closed answer set made it look tractable.

It wasn't. On broadcast frames the bumper text is a handful of pixels tall, and no amount of voting recovers digits that were never resolved. Identity is now one tap per robot by the scout, helped by robot photos and path suggestions, and OCR is gone from the system.

sections.h: The pivot: why broadcast video lost

blocks.html: For most of the project the vision pipeline ran on the server, against event broadcasts. It would download the stream, calibrate automatically from the field's AprilTags, track every robot, and read bumper numbers. On September 25 it ran end to end in production for the first time.

Then I checked the output by eye. On the best Championship feed, 6 of the 15 tracks it had identified mixed up two robots from the same alliance. Each robot was also only covered for a fraction of the match. Every 2026 broadcast is split-screen, so robots are small and bumper text is smaller still. Nothing downstream could fix that. The information wasn't in the pixels.

So on September 28 I retired it: stream extraction, server-side tracking, bumper OCR, broadcast calibration, and the worker container that ran them. Vision moved onto the scout's phone, filmed from the stands where robots are bigger and a person can say which is which. The server image went from about 11 GB to 1.65 GB.
It was the right call and an uncomfortable one. That pipeline was months of work, and it did run. It just didn't produce data I'd let a strategy team act on.

General-purpose detectors barely register competition robots. They aren't in the training distribution of a model trained on everyday objects. The detector here is single-class, trained on match footage. The early versions learned from 6,540 labeled frames with a reviewed subset of 1,683 images.

blocks.alt: A FIRST Robotics broadcast frame with three robots marked by lime detection boxes across a foreshortened field.
blocks.label: Reviewed frame · 03 detections
blocks.cap: A relatively clean broadcast view. Even here, the robots occupy only a small fraction of the frame and the sponsor panel obscures the center foreground.

blocks.alt: A crowded FIRST Robotics broadcast frame with robots marked by detection boxes across the main view and two picture-in-picture views.
blocks.label: Reviewed frame · crowded field
blocks.cap: The harder case: robots cross, shrink into the far field, and appear again in picture-in-picture views. These are annotations from the real-broadcast dataset, not a staged visualization.

blocks.html: The v1 run scored 98.0% mAP@50 on its validation split, which sounds finished and isn't. That split is drawn from the same events, the same venues, and often the same matches as the training data. It measures whether the model learned the frames it was shown. It says very little about a competition it has never seen.

So one full event, Einstein 2026, was held out entirely and locked as a benchmark. Against that, the same model scored 69.9%. That drop is the real measurement, and it's the one that governs whether a new model ships. v2 was promoted because it reached 71.7% on that locked holdout, not because its loss curves looked better.
Before reading why recall stalled, try the job the labels were meant to do. These are real frames from the training data.

blocks.text: Detector v4: the labels were the bug

blocks.html: After v2, recall wouldn't move. Dropping the confidence threshold to almost nothing still left it around half, which is what you'd expect if the model believed some robots were background. It did, because that's what it had been taught.

An audit of the training labels found they boxed about 3.31 robots per frame, when a typical frame actually holds about 5.2. Every robot left unboxed was a lesson that robots look like background. More training on those labels would only have taught it more firmly.

The fix was to train only on frames whose labels were already near-complete: 798 for training and 156 for validation, plus 45 missing robots I confirmed by eye. Model proposals were never auto-accepted, because at high confidence only about 40% of them were real robots. Four training runs on one rented A100 took 3 h 23 min and cost $6.73, and the instance shut itself down when they finished.

On the same locked holdout, with both models re-measured at full 1280-pixel resolution (which is why v2 reads slightly differently here than above), mAP@50 went from 71.9% to 77.9% and recall from 51% to 68%. On real stands footage it now finds 3.95 robots per frame, against 2.8 to 3.2 before.

blocks.s: Precision 91%, recall 68%, and why that tradeoff is still the right one

blocks.html: On the holdout, v4 is precise and still somewhat conservative: when it calls something a robot it's almost always right, and it misses about a third of the ones it isn't sure about. For this system that's the correct direction to err.

A missed detection is a gap the tracker can bridge and the scout can see. A false detection is a phantom robot with a path, a zone history, and a heat map attributed to a real team. That noise propagates and looks exactly like real data. Recall went up because the labels got fixed, not because precision was traded away for it.

sections.h: Running a neural network on a phone

blocks.html: Moving vision onto the phone only works if a full match finishes before the next one starts. The first version took about seven minutes on a CPU. It now takes well under one.
Four changes did most of it:

items: Read only the field. A stands view is a thin strip, so a square model input was mostly padding. The detector now reads just the calibrated field area, which is about twice as fast and finds more robots because they're bigger in the input.

Use every core. WebAssembly can run on several threads, but only on a page with stricter browser isolation. The recorder runs on its own isolated page, so the rest of the app can keep embedding match videos.
Decode, don't play. Frames used to come from playing the video in real time. WebCodecs now decodes them straight from the file, which took an uploaded match from 85 s to 33 s on a GPU.
Pick the engine per device. WebGPU gets the full-size model. CPU devices get the nano model, which in WebKit takes 82 ms a frame against 243 ms for the full one.

blocks.html: These are measured on a laptop in Chrome and in WebKit, the engine Safari and every iPhone browser use. A full run on a real phone at a real event is the next test, and I'll say so until it's done.

Detection says where robots are. The scout says who they are, and the goal is to ask as little as possible. To measure that, I labelled one match by hand from its 1080p upload: bumper numbers, each robot's look, and elimination within a frame.

Against those labels, conservative stitching cut one match from 126 path fragments to 81, with 95.7% of hand labels landing on the right team. Looser rules made fewer fragments and much worse identity, so they didn't ship. Path suggestions then cut the scout's taps from 81 to 48. The trade is that about one suggestion in ten is wrong, and the screen says that rather than hiding it.

blocks.s: The run that said "done" at 89 seconds

blocks.html: Under detection load, WebKit silently drops a video's source every couple of minutes. The stall watchdog read that as the end of the match, so a breakdown covering only the first 89 seconds was reported as complete, with 66 paths and no warning.

The recorder now reopens the file and resumes from the last frame it processed, and if the video keeps failing it says how far it got. A silent partial result is the worst kind, because it looks like a finished one.
FRCMOB predicts who wins each match, and every page that shows a win probability shows the same one. Getting that number right meant first admitting a wrong one.

The machine-learning model I'd built scored 82% in training. Tested properly, rating each team only from events it had already played, it scored 49.8%. That's a coin flip, and worse than the plain formula's 59.2%. The 82% was leakage: the end-of-event ratings it learned from already contained the matches it was predicting.

The fix was an as-of replay. For each match, the database is rewound to what was known before it, and only that is used to predict it. Run over the 56 newest events of the 2026 season, it scored every candidate on exactly the same replay.

blocks.cap: 2,507 held-out matches · each predicted from earlier results only
rows: Fuel rate, shrunk toward last event (shipped)

blocks.html: The shipped predictor is simple. Each team's official fuel rate from its earlier matches at the event is shrunk toward its rate at its previous event, harder when it has played fewer matches. The alliance sums are compared and turned into a probability with one scale factor, fitted on over 15,000 matches from older events. Teams with no fuel history fall back to the rating formula.

The lesson is the last row of that table. Fed inputs computed after the matches, even the simple formula looked like 81.5%, and on the first round of each event, before any result existed, it scored 82%. With those inputs removed, that same round fell to a coin flip. Every evaluation now cuts post-match data off first, and the ML stays switched off in production until it beats the formula on the same replay.
The vision work gets the attention, but most of what a team touches at an event is everything around it. Venue wifi fails, scouts swap phones, and a lead needs to know who is watching which robot.

items: Join with a 10-character code, stored only as a hash
Picklists, pit notes and rooms stay private to the team
Removing a member takes effect on every request
One room per team per event
The lead assigns scouts to robots, match by match, saved atomically
Live sync over WebSockets and Redis, about 0.8 s phone to phone
"Ready for no signal": schedules, ratings, predictions and team pages saved ahead
Edits queue offline and replay in order
Match alerts, Match Center with live scores
Picklists with a live alliance-selection mode
Pit scouting, strategy briefings, Alliance Advisor

blocks.html: There are also native iOS and Android apps, built with Capacitor, that keep their sign-in tokens in the Keychain and Keystore. They're built and tested, not in the stores yet.

blocks.cap: The full tap-first scouting surface with no connection. The match form stays available and the banner makes local saving explicit instead of failing silently.

blocks.alt: The FRCMOB autonomous path editor showing field zones and a curved blue route across the field.
blocks.label: Auto path drawer · spatial evidence

blocks.html: Once the video work moved onto phones, the server stopped needing to be big. It needs to be close to its database, fast on venue connections, and cheap enough to leave running all season.

items: Postgres and Redis on the VM

blocks.alt: Jamal at a workbench in the robotics lab with a laptop open to a terminal session on the deployment server.
blocks.label: Plate 01
blocks.cap: Working on the Oracle Cloud deployment that runs the backend. The screen is deliberately obscured here; it was an SSH session into the deployment host.

blocks.html: The whole backend runs on one free Oracle Cloud VM, with 4 cores and 24 GB of memory, for $0 a month. On it are the FastAPI app, Postgres 17, Redis 7, and Caddy for HTTPS. There's no separate worker any more. The React and TypeScript frontend is on Vercel with edge caching in front of the API, and an hourly off-site backup goes to Neon.
The frontend is built offline-first. Scouts lose connectivity constantly in a venue, so submissions queue locally and sync when the network comes back rather than failing.

blocks.s: Keeping the phone and the server in agreement

blocks.html: The phone's breakdown has to agree with what the server does with it afterwards, which is a real risk when similar logic exists in two languages. The tracking and stitching code is benchmarked against a hand-labelled match, so a change that makes paths look tidier but puts robots on the wrong team fails a number rather than slipping through.
The backend had been off since April. On September 24 I brought it back on the free VM, and most of what followed was learning what only breaks for real.

Distance was the slow part. The database and Redis were managed services in another region, so every query paid a long round trip. Moving both onto the VM took a schedule request from 911 ms to 18 ms and event ratings from 784 ms to 36 ms.

blocks.s: The backup that broke the app

blocks.html: A database backup taken through Neon's connection pooler changed a session setting, and the pooler handed that broken setting to the app's own connections. The app couldn't find its tables until it was fixed. The backup script now refuses to run against the pooler at all.

blocks.s: Room bugs that only real two-phone tests found

blocks.html: Production runs two server processes; my laptop ran one. Joining a room and opening its live connection could land on different processes, and when they did, the connection was refused as a duplicate scout. The fix clears a scout's presence in Redis, which both processes share, and a new test runs two hubs against one shared store to prove it.

The same tests found a second one: reopening a room from another device within 30 seconds was rejected as a duplicate, 12 times out of 12. The check behind it predated team workspaces, when scouts picked their own names. Since workspaces, it could only ever match the same person, so it was removed.

blocks.s: Speed work

items: Edge caching turned a 0.81 s miss into a 0.18 s hit.
One slow endpoint went from 2.9 s to 10 ms.
Real-user speed timings are now collected, so the next round starts from data.

blocks.s: Cleanup from production logs

blocks.html: One scheduled job re-downloaded the same data every 3 hours and rewrote the same 1,662 rows. Another rebuilt pages for finished events every 2 minutes, for 60 to 100 seconds a run, which kept about half a server process busy for data that couldn't change. The first is gone; the second now only rebuilds events that are in play.
A full re-ingest of the 2026 season finished 299 of 299 events with no failures, unattended.

Eight browser guards sweep the app and fail on colours outside the palette, off-scale type sizes, weak contrast, overflow, missing affordances, and pages in one section that don't look like each other.

The consistency guard only ran at desktop width, so drift that showed up only on phones passed it. I extended it to phone width and checked that it fails on the old code before trusting it on the new. Under the guards sit about 1,400 automated tests across the backend and frontend.

When analysis finishes, the system generates a draft scouting form per team rather than a final record. Fields carry per-field confidence and are marked ready or low-confidence, so a reviewer knows where to look first instead of re-checking everything equally.

A scout approves the draft, overrides specific fields, or rejects it with a reason, and those decisions are kept. The plan is to use override rates per field to check the confidence estimates: a field marked high-confidence that humans keep correcting is miscalibrated, and a field nobody touches can have its threshold raised.

That calibration hasn't run yet. There aren't enough reviewed drafts to tune anything on evidence, so for now the thresholds are judgment, and I'd rather say that than imply a loop that hasn't closed.

blocks.s: Ratings that mean something across events

blocks.html: A raw score doesn't compare across events, because event fields differ in strength. Ratings are normalized against the rest of the field at that event, with outliers trimmed, and carry a confidence derived from how many matches back them.
Teams with little match data are anchored with an external prior that's blended out as real data accumulates, so early-event ratings aren't wild guesses dressed up as measurements.

blocks.s: Shipping a model without breaking the one in use

blocks.html: Model changes are deployed in shadow first: the candidate runs alongside what's in production, its predictions are logged, and nothing it says reaches a user. Promotion is a decision made on a fixed comparison, not on a feeling.

That process did its job. The match-outcome model is switched off in production because it lost a fair test to a simpler formula, as described in predicting matches without hindsight. Without a benchmark fixed in advance, "the new model seems better" is an easy thing to believe and hard to check.

blocks.s: A season-specific game, a system that has to outlive it

blocks.html: FRC changes its game every year: different scoring, different field, different roles. Season-specific rules are isolated into their own configuration and game-context layer instead of being spread through the analysis code, so a new season is a configuration change plus retraining rather than a rewrite. The system refuses to run on a season it doesn't know rather than guessing.

blocks.s: Degraded runs that announce themselves

blocks.html: Pipelines fail quietly by default: a bad calibration, a video that stopped halfway, or a model that didn't load still produces output, just wrong output. Runs carry quality signals, and a run that is partial or produced too few findings says so rather than being reported as ordinary.

The backend has been live since September. Recall is up, and the on-device breakdown is now the main path, not a fallback. The parts I'd call solid are the as-of evaluation setup for both the detector and the predictor, team rooms and offline sync, and the production deployment.
The open work, in the order I care about it:

items: A full match on a real phone at a real event. So far the on-device numbers come from desktop browsers and emulated phones.
Native apps in the stores. Signing, push notifications, and App Store and Play Store setup.
Optional sign-in by email code. Designed and built, switched off until there's a domain to send from.
2027 season readiness. The system already refuses to run on unknown seasons. A new game needs its rules, its scoring, and a detector retrain.
ML that earns its place. A model using only pre-match features reached 72.6% in testing, but it isn't switched on. It goes live when it beats the shipped formula on the same as-of replay, not before.

head.html: An auditing and remediation system for Windows and Windows Server. It inspects system state, reports what's wrong as evidence, applies security policy against a baseline, and makes sure there's a way back before it changes anything.

rows: CyberPatriot XVIII Open Division National Semifinalist, January 2026

head.html: This page describes how the system is built and why. It leaves out specific checks, registry paths, and detection logic on purpose. That detail is more useful to someone evading controls than to someone evaluating the engineering.

blocks.html: CyberPatriot hands you a compromised Windows image and a clock. Somewhere in it are misconfigured policies, unauthorized accounts, disabled protections, and things installed to persist. You find and fix as much as you can before time runs out.

Doing that by hand doesn't scale. The check list runs to hundreds of items across authentication, accounts, services, firewall, Defender, and audit policy. Under time pressure, people skip checks and misread state. Then there's the expensive mistake: applying a change that breaks the machine or locks you out of the account you're working from. A wrong move on account policy can end a round.

The obvious response is to script it. The trap is that a script which blindly applies settings is more dangerous than doing nothing, because it makes the destructive mistake faster and across more of the system at once.

blocks.alt: A PowerShell console during a CyberPatriot round, filled with repeated red Set-NetFirewallProfile errors reading 'There are no more endpoints available from the endpoint mapper'.
blocks.label: Plate 01 — competition machine, 14 Dec 2025
blocks.cap: What that looks like in practice. Set-NetFirewallProfile failing repeatedly with Windows System Error 1753 because the endpoint mapper had been tampered with on the image. The run keeps going and logs the failure rather than stopping, which is the behaviour the framework is built around.

blocks.html: The design rule the whole thing follows: the tool must be able to tell you what's wrong without changing anything. Every check is written so it can run in either mode: report the finding, or report it and fix it. Simulate is the default. You have to ask for changes, and confirm them.

That inversion is what makes the automation usable. You run the read-only pass, get a scorecard, discover that your authorized-user list was missing a service account, fix the list, and run again, all before the machine has been touched. The mistakes happen in the findings, not on the system.

The checks are organized as modules against CIS-style baselines, with separate baselines for workstation and for Windows Server 2019 and 2022. The same check often has a different correct answer depending on what the machine is for.

Most of the effort went into not causing damage. Applying a registry change is one line of PowerShell. Applying hundreds of them under time pressure without breaking the machine is what the rest of the code is for.

blocks.s: Every destructive run writes its own undo

blocks.html: Before a run modifies anything, it captures the relevant current state and generates a revert script from it. Nobody has to remember a rollback procedure: the script sits next to the backup, built from what the machine looked like a moment ago.

blocks.s: Account changes require a declared policy

blocks.html: User, administrator, and remote-access management is the most dangerous surface in the tool, because removing the wrong account is both easy and hard to undo from a locked-out session.

So the tool won't infer who belongs. Authorized accounts are declared in explicit lists, and the simulate pass shows you exactly which accounts a run would touch before it touches them. The documentation is blunt about this being the step where people hurt themselves.

blocks.s: Staged aggression

blocks.html: There's a difference between the changes that are almost always right and the long tail of baseline items that are correct in principle and occasionally break something specific to the image.

Those are separated. The standard pass applies the well-understood set. Full baseline remediation is a distinct, opt-in mode documented as a last step, run only after a clean standard pass. That way a broad sweep can't be the thing that breaks a machine you hadn't finished checking.

blocks.s: Everything produces evidence

blocks.html: Each run writes a timestamped log, a pass/fail scorecard, and per-area CSV findings covering what was inspected and what was changed. Partly that's for scoring a competition round; mostly it's because a security tool whose actions you can't audit is a security problem of its own.
Bravo Prime reached the CyberPatriot XVIII National Semifinals, held online from 22 to 24 January 2026. After the opening day we were sitting 15th in the nation within Open Division, Platinum tier.

Two things about that 15th. It was scoped to Open Division, Platinum tier, not to every team in the competition. And it was a first-day standing, not a final placement, because scores move a lot over the remaining rounds and ours did too. The screenshot below is one leaderboard on one morning, not our final result.

blocks.alt: A CyberPatriot leaderboard extract showing row 15, team 18-4257, Texas, Open Division, Platinum tier.
blocks.label: Plate 02 — opening-day standings, National Semifinals
blocks.cap: Row 15 is us: team 18-4257, Texas, Open Division, Platinum tier. Opening day of the National Semifinals only.

blocks.html: The framework is around 11,900 lines of PowerShell across roughly 170 functions. The size comes from coverage: hundreds of checks, each written in an audit form and a remediation form, across three target configurations, with backup and rollback around the ones that change state.

The structure is what keeps it maintainable: baselines live in data files rather than in code, so adding or adjusting a check doesn't mean editing control flow. Windows Server 2019 and 2022 have their own registry mappings, and the target is selected at run time.

The competition framing made one lesson unavoidable: an automated system that acts on production state has to be designed on the assumption that it will sometimes be wrong, because the machine will eventually be in a state you didn't plan for.

Read-only by default, explicit confirmation, generated rollback, and recorded evidence are what make it reasonable to let a script make hundreds of security decisions on a system you care about. That's the same principle the review loop in FRCMOB is built on, arrived at from a completely different direction.

head.html: A course for developers and QA engineers, built around a problem most cryptography teaching avoids: deciding whether software that uses cryptography is safe to ship.

rows: Practical Cryptography for Developers and QA Engineers

head.html: Instructor materials, hidden assessment tests, and the capstone source aren't published here. The capstone is intentionally vulnerable training software and is meant to run only on a student's own machine.

sections.h: The gap this is aimed at

blocks.html: A developer can pass a cryptography quiz and still ship something broken. They know AES is a block cipher and that you shouldn't reuse an IV, and then they read code that reuses one and don't notice, because recognizing the mistake in unfamiliar software is a different skill from reciting the rule.

Almost nothing about real cryptographic failure is about the algorithms. AES doesn't break. What breaks is everything around it: a mode chosen for the wrong reason, a nonce derived predictably, a signature verified in a code path nobody takes, a token whose algorithm field is trusted. Those are integration and review failures, and you don't catch them by knowing definitions.
So the course is built backwards from what a working engineer has to do: look at a system, work out where cryptography appears in it, test whether it holds, and say whether it ships.
43 lectures across 16 sections. The first half builds the mechanics; the second half is progressively less about how primitives work and more about how they get misused.
Heartbleed, DigiNotar, and the rest get whole sections because a student who has seen how a real system failed reads unfamiliar code differently than one who has only seen it work.

The lecture pipeline renders concepts as timed visual explanations, not screenshot-heavy slides. These frames come directly from the course's render checks; each one has to carry the argument even with the narration muted.

blocks.alt: Course frame explaining that finding any matching pair takes roughly the square root of the work of hitting one fixed target.
blocks.label: Collision resistance
blocks.cap: The birthday effect turns an abstract exponent into a comparison students can see.

blocks.alt: Course frame comparing accidental corruption with attacker-chosen input when deciding whether MD5 is acceptable.
blocks.label: Threat modeling
blocks.cap: The useful question is not only which algorithm, but who controls the input.

blocks.alt: Course frame mapping file integrity, signatures, passwords, and keyed hashes to modern cryptographic choices.
blocks.label: Replacement choices
blocks.cap: Different jobs need different primitives; “use SHA-256” is not a complete rule.

blocks.html: Students are handed a release candidate: a production-shaped B2B document portal with an API, a browser client, a TLS gateway, and cryptography threaded through it in the places you'd expect. It comes with a smoke suite that passes.

That last detail is the whole design. The supplied tests prove the ordinary workflows run. They prove nothing about whether the release is secure, and the course is explicit that students shouldn't confuse the two. A green test suite on insecure software is exactly the situation this is training for.
The assignment is the real job, in order:

items: Find where cryptography appears in a system nobody explained to you.
Build a testing framework specific to what this system actually does.
Write and run executable tests. Running code, not a written review.
Report what's wrong, with enough support that someone else can act on it.
Make a defensible release decision, and defend it.

blocks.s: Why the defects are planted on purpose

blocks.html: Because I know every defect in the application, there's a ground truth for what a thorough audit should surface. A student's work gets measured against what's there, not against how confident their report sounds.
It also means I got to pick the failure modes. They come from the categories that cause real incidents, not the ones that are convenient to hide.

blocks.s: Grading a security audit without a right answer key

blocks.html: Assessment runs against hidden tests rather than a rubric a student can pattern-match. Alongside that, mutation-based evaluation checks something a checklist can't: whether a student's test suite detects the problems it claims to cover.
A test that passes on broken code is worse than no test, because it produces confidence. Mutating the system and checking that the student's tests fail is how you find that out.

Lectures alone don't teach you to spot a broken implementation, so the course ships a local range: 16 graded exercises plus an orientation, roughly 14 hours of work, placed at the points in the course where a new skill becomes testable.

It borrows the rhythm of a cyber competition. Read a scenario, inspect a real artifact on your own machine, make a decision you have to defend, repair something when the exercise asks for it, and watch the score report update. No virtual machine, no cloud account, and nothing that needs production credentials or a system you don't own.

Sixteen exercises, sixteen different formats. A key-ceremony tabletop and a mutation-test design exercise assess different things, and running everything as the same kind of quiz would flatten that.

blocks.s: Why the range runs on your own machine

blocks.html: Every exercise runs from an extracted folder with a private Python environment, on Python 3.11+. Setup is one script, and it prints READY or tells you what's wrong.

The reason is access. A course that needs a cloud account or a VM image excludes people, breaks when a provider changes, and puts a billing question between a student and the material. A folder and a Python install keeps working.
The last deliverable is a judgment: does this ship, and why?

That's the part I most wanted in the course, because it's the part engineers get wrong and no exam tests. Not every defect blocks a release, and "I found something" is not a decision. The skill is working out which findings block, which are acceptable with a known risk, and how to say so to someone who wants to ship on Friday. That's what separates someone who can run a scanner from someone you'd trust to sign off.
It's also the same idea underneath FRCMOB's review loop and the simulate-first design of the hardening framework: an automated result is evidence for a decision, not the decision.

head.html: A student-run program that teaches free robotics camps for grades 3–8, using kits the club has developed over several generations. I run the program. I did not design the kits, and this page is mostly about the hard part: getting a room full of ten-year-olds to finish a working robot and understand what they just did.

Eaglets is a team effort across a rotating group of student officers, and the kit lineage below predates me. Where this page says "the program" or "the team," that is not me. My own responsibilities are camps, curriculum, officer training, and keeping the sessions free.

blocks.html: Off-the-shelf educational robots solve the wrong problem. The good ones are expensive enough that a free camp can't buy a classroom set. The cheap ones are either toys that don't teach programming, or bare components that lose a beginner before anything moves.

So the program builds its own. That turns a teaching problem into a hardware and software problem with unusual constraints. The kit has to be cheap enough to buy in quantity and rugged enough to be assembled, disassembled, and dropped by a rotating cast of elementary schoolers. It has to go from a box of parts to a moving robot within a session, because a camp doesn't get a second day to recover a lost room.
And the code a nine-year-old writes on day one has to do something visible, without hiding so much that they haven't learned anything. That last constraint is the one that shapes the software.
Each version came out of something that went wrong at a camp.

blocks.alt: The first Eaglets robot kit, with a breadboard controller, ultrasonic sensor, and exposed wiring on a black chassis.

blocks.html: The proof that the whole idea was viable: a younger student could build and program it inside a single session.

blocks.alt: The second Eaglets robot kit viewed from above, with a Raspberry Pi Pico and motor driver mounted on a wooden chassis.

blocks.html: Rebuilt around the exact steps where students got stuck in the early camps.

blocks.alt: Eaglets kit version 3.2 with a wooden chassis, sensors, motors, battery, and hand-wired electronics.

blocks.html: An ultrasonic distance sensor and a photoresistor. This is where students start writing conditions, like turning when a wall gets close, instead of fixed sequences.

blocks.alt: Eaglets kit version 3.6 beside its laser-cut wooden lid, showing the Pico controller, sensors, and wiring.

blocks.html: The version that ran the season, with the revision silkscreened onto the chassis so a kit in a bin is identifiable years later.
The PCBs broke mid-season with camps already booked across Texas. The team rebuilt on breadboards and kept teaching. The controller and motor drive changed three times as the season went on.
The first generation with a proper KiCad design and a schematic on file, rather than a layout that existed mainly in the head of whoever built it.
The generation being prepared for testing and summer 2027 production. It isn't finished yet.

The V5 board appears in a bill of materials, but its design files couldn't be located. Either it lives somewhere outside the shared drive, or kits were built from something that was never checked in. Rather than guess, it's left out of the lineage above.
Mid-season in 2025, with camps already booked across Texas, the PCBs failed. Cancelling wasn't an option, because those camps were the program.

The team rebuilt on breadboards and kept going, and the design changed under them three times as the season ran. The first camps drove motors through transistors, which turned out to be the weak point and became a motor driver. The controller moved to Arduino and back to Raspberry Pi Pico once it could be supported again. The LEDs got cut, because a Pico takes up most of a breadboard and something had to go.

It would be easy to tell the breadboard switch as a teaching decision: students see the circuit, so wiring becomes part of the lesson. That isn't what happened. The boards broke, the team improvised under a deadline, and the camps ran anyway.

sections.h: Software a beginner can get through

blocks.html: I've worked on the beginner-facing libraries and taught Python and C++ at camps. The design question that never goes away is how much to hide.

blocks.alt: Jamal speaking from a podium at an Eaglets camp session, with the program's slide projected behind him.
blocks.label: Plate 03
blocks.cap: Running a session at an Eaglets camp. Photographs from camps are cropped to exclude students.

blocks.html: Wrap too little and a beginner spends the session on pin configuration and PWM and never gets the robot to move. Wrap too much and you've built a toy where go_forward() is the whole lesson, and the student succeeds without understanding anything transferable.

The line we've settled on: hide the register-level setup, expose the logic. A student writes the condition that decides what happens when the distance sensor reads under some threshold. They don't write the ultrasonic timing code, but the decision is theirs, and it's a real one. Sensors are what make that possible, and they're usually where students stop copying code and start debugging it.

blocks.s: Debugging teaches the most

blocks.html: The moment worth engineering for is when a student's robot does something they didn't intend. That's when they have to reason about what the code actually says versus what they meant, which is the skill that carries.
It also means the kit has to fail in ways a beginner can see. A robot that stops silently teaches nothing. One that visibly turns the wrong way gives a student something to chase.

Eaglets turns over its entire leadership every year, which is the defining constraint on how it's run. Every officer group inherits an organization from people who have graduated, and anything that only exists in someone's head is lost at the handoff.
What I'm responsible for right now:

items: Rebuilding the 2026–27 team. Recruiting into open officer roles and training new officers, with the assumption that they'll arrive with no context.
V6 development. Preparing the current kit generation for testing and summer 2027 production. V6 is not production-ready yet.
Season planning. Building the curriculum, logistics, and volunteer capacity needed for the summer 2027 program.
Grants and partnerships. Funding and the organizational relationships that keep camps free.
Technical continuity. Making sure design decisions are written down where the next officer team will find them, which is the only thing that stops the program relearning the same lessons.

blocks.html: None of that is what I expected the job to be. Most of the technical work turns out to be documentation and handoff. An organization that forgets why the boards broke will design the same failure again.

head.html: Allen Eagle Robotics builds a new competition robot every year on a six-week clock. I work fabrication during build season and the pit during events. In February 2026 I began building FRCMOB for the team, and Team 5417 has since used the platform at a real competition.
The awards below were won by the team. I was a member of it, and that's how they're stated.

blocks.html: FRC gives every team the same rough shape of problem: a game is announced, and about six weeks later you need a working robot. I came in on the fabrication side, making and assembling the parts that become the machine, through a build season where the design is still changing around you.

At competition I work the pit. That's the turnaround between matches: battery swaps, checking the robot over, fixing whatever came loose, and getting it back out on the field in time for the next one. It's unglamorous and it's the difference between three matches and six.

Being in the pit is also how I ended up writing software for the team. You hear every strategy conversation that happens between matches, and you notice how thin the information behind those decisions actually is.

I began FRCMOB in February 2026 because the team needed a better way to collect and use match evidence. It supports multiple scouts, offline submissions, and strategy analysis, and Team 5417 has used it at a real competition.

What made it grow was watching the limits of that approach from the pit. Scouting data is only as good as the attention of the person filling out the form, and six robots move at once for two and a half minutes. The gaps were always in the same place: the teams nobody was assigned to watch were often the ones you most needed to know about by alliance selection.

The footage, meanwhile, has all of it. That's the observation behind the computer-vision work in FRCMOB. I am still improving its auto-scouting, offline collection, mobile reliability, model evaluation, and strategy tools.
Fabrication taught me the other half of it. A part that works on the bench and fails at competition is a part that failed, and nobody cares why. That's the same standard I hold the software to.

head.html: A native macOS menu-bar app that records the meeting you explicitly approve, transcribes it on-device, and leaves behind notes you can edit. Its most important feature is the recording it refuses to start by itself.
The repository is private. This case study documents the architecture, privacy boundary, and verified behavior without publishing meeting data, prompts, credentials, or private source.

blocks.html: Meeting automation has an unusually sharp failure mode: convenience can become silent recording. Notetaker treats detection and consent as two different events. Seeing Zoom's in-meeting helper process or a live meeting title is enough to show a prompt. It is never enough to begin capture.

In the code there is exactly one path that begins capture, and it is reachable from two places: the menu bar item you click, and the button in a dialog you answered. Detection can raise that dialog. It cannot answer it. That asymmetry is on purpose: a recorder that starts itself in a 1:1 or an interview is not a bug you get to apologize for afterward.

Stopping is the opposite. Leaving the meeting ends the recording on its own, since forgetting to press stop costs you nothing worse than a longer file, while forgetting to press start costs you the meeting. Convenience belongs on whichever side of a decision is harmless when it fires by accident.

That distinction survives the whole design. Audio stays on the Mac. whisper.cpp produces a local transcript. Only after recording stops does a single text-only request turn that transcript into decisions and action items. The editable Markdown result stays beside the source transcript.

sections.h: A small app with a real pipeline

blocks.html: The stream combines system audio, the people on the other side, with microphone input. A discarded 2×2 pixel region satisfies the capture API without turning the app into a screen recorder.
Audio is converted to 16 kHz mono WAV so the transcription stage gets one predictable format regardless of the devices active in the meeting.
Transcription runs locally. A meeting topic, sanitized before it can become a folder name, gives the final summarizer enough context to produce a useful heading and clearer notes.

sections.h: The bug that looked like success

blocks.html: Audio software can hand back a perfectly valid file while recording the wrong thing. ScreenCaptureKit has a flag calledexcludesCurrentProcessAudio, and setting it true reads like obvious hygiene: don't capture your own app's output. On macOS 26 it silently kills the entire system-audio tap.

The measured peak amplitude of the system channel drops from 0.78 to exactly 0.0. Every surface-level check still passes. The file exists, the RIFF header is well formed, the duration is right, and the waveform looks normal because your microphone is still feeding it. What you have lost is every other participant. With headphones on, the failure is total and invisible: you record yourself saying "mm-hm" for forty minutes and nothing else.

That is the reason the WAV harness drives the writer with two synthetic tones instead of asserting that a file was produced. It starts a 440 Hz tone at zero seconds and an 880 Hz tone one second later, then measures RMS in three windows: the first source alone, the overlap, and the second source alone. The overlap has to be meaningfully louder than either tone by itself, which is only true if mixing actually happened. It also checks that summed peaks clamp instead of wrapping around, because a sign inversion at the top of the range is the kind of thing you hear as a click and never find by reading code.
Inspect the output structure and measured signal, not just file creation.
Exercise the meeting signal separately from the permission to record.
Test slashes, colons, and newlines before calendar text becomes a path.

blocks.s: What the app won't guess

blocks.html: whisper.cpp does not provide reliable speaker diarization here, so the note prompt only attributes a statement when context makes the speaker clear. A missing label beats a confident wrong one.
Both of these look correct in documentation and fail against a real machine. They cost me more time than the parts that worked, so they are written down.

blocks.s: Asking the audio system whether the microphone is in use

blocks.html: kAudioDevicePropertyDeviceIsRunningSomewhere sounds like exactly the right meeting signal. If something is holding the microphone, you are probably in a call, and it would work across every platform at once without caring which app is running.

On macOS 26 it reports false while an application is actively recording. I checked it against ffmpeg holding the microphone open, so this is measured, not inferred. Any detector built on it would have failed closed and never prompted at all.

blocks.s: Reading Zoom's own meeting data

blocks.html: Zoom keeps meeting databases under its application support directory, which would supply participant lists and real scheduled topics instead of whatever the window happens to be called. Every one of those files is encrypted on disk.

That leaves the window title as the only local source of a meeting name. Getting participants would mean a Zoom OAuth application and cloud API calls, which trades a local-only tool for one that needs account credentials and network access. For an app whose entire premise is that your audio never leaves the machine, that is a bad trade, so the feature stays missing.

This is a useful personal tool, not a general meeting platform. Rebuilding the app can cause macOS to ask for capture permission again because the code identity changes. Transcription speed and quality depend on the local model and the audio. Participant names are unavailable without adding a Zoom cloud integration, which would create a much larger privacy and authentication surface than this app currently needs.

head.html: A macOS agent that understands an interface nobody gave it an API for. It captures a window, reads it with Vision OCR, falls back to measured colour where the interface is icons, and drives it with synthesized input. It happens to be pointed at a game. The interesting part is everything between capture and click.

This automates a Roblox game, which violates Roblox's Terms of Service. The repository says so up front, and so does this page. There's a full section on it below, because deciding what a tool is allowed to do is part of building one.

sections.h: Reading an interface you have no API for

blocks.html: The general problem is more interesting than the specific one. You have a running application. You cannot query it, you cannot read its memory, and you cannot change its code. All you get is what it draws. From that, you have to work out what state it is in and what to do next, reliably enough to run unattended for hours and safely enough that being wrong means doing nothing instead of doing damage.

The rule I set at the start was that the macro only ever looks at pixels and only ever sends the input a person could send. No memory reading, no injection, no modified client. That pushes every hard question into computer vision and state modeling, where the answers can be measured, and keeps them out of a debugger, where they'd just be brittle.

The obvious approach to a UI you can't query is template matching: cut a PNG of each button, then hunt for it. It works right up until the window changes size, at which point you need one template per control per resolution and a small archive of images to maintain.

Reading the text instead survives all of that. A resize moves the button; it does not rename it. Coordinates are stored as fractions of the window rather than pixels, so the same rules hold at another size. What it does not survive is the game changing its wording. That's the expected failure mode, so classification rules live in one file and the recorded captures double as the regression suite.

Reading costs real time, so there are two tiers. Parsing the fixed HUD bands takes about 308 ms; classifying a whole frame takes about 1.01 s. The loop polls the cheap one and pays for the expensive one only when a menu might be open, a restart is due, or a finished stage could be hiding an overlay behind the HUD.
Vision returns Cyrillic lookalikes for Latin letters often enough to break exact matching: Epic comes back as Еріс. Everything compared against a known word is folded first.
Patterns match substrings and the first hit wins. A rewards list containing "Currency - End run reward" was being found before the End Run button, so button patterns are anchored.
Screen identity uses fuzzy token matching. One character read differently between frames drops strict set comparison below any sane threshold, and the same screen gets recorded over and over.

blocks.s: The exception that proves the anchoring rule

blocks.html: Anchored patterns are right everywhere except one screen, where the button reads New Run (0/1). An anchored pattern can never match a counter suffix, so that single case is a prefix match. In a diff it looks like an inconsistency, but it's the only pattern that matches.

One screen defeats all of it. The Route Atlas, the map you pick your next floor from, is drawn entirely as icons. There is no text on any node, so OCR returns nothing to click. The only signal left is colour, and the game hands you the encoding itself, in a legend printed beside the map.

blocks.alt: The Odyssey Route Atlas: a branching graph of icon nodes, bright near the centre and dim toward the bottom, with a colour legend printed in a panel on the right.
blocks.label: Plate 01
blocks.cap: One of the sixteen recorded atlas captures. Progression runs up the screen, so the current floor is the lowest bright node and the choices are the bright row directly above it. The dim nodes below are history. A capture like this is where the thresholds came from, and the same file is now a test fixture.

blocks.html: Both rules that matter here were measured off that capture, and both are easy to get wrong from first principles. Red is hue 1, not hue 178, because red wraps around zero in OpenCV's 0–180 hue space. And red and white sit at the same hue, so what separates an Elite floor from a Battle floor is saturation: 167 against 0.

The brightness threshold is the one that would have been a silent bug. Visited floors are still drawn, just dimmer, and they sit below the current floor on the screen. Without a value cutoff the macro would happily pick one and route itself backwards through floors it had already played. That's a run that never ends and never progresses, and from the outside it looks exactly like working software.

sections.h: Three failures that only appear hours in

blocks.html: Everything above can be checked in a test. These three could not. Each one only showed up when the thing ran for real, overnight or as an installed application, and each is written down in the repository so nobody, including me, has to rediscover it.

blocks.text: A leak inside a single Core Graphics call

blocks.html: The macro ran overnight and was killed by macOS. Memory had grown to 83,643 MB. The cause was one function: wrapping each captured frame for Vision with CGDataProviderCreateWithData pinned a full ~5.2 MB RGBA buffer per OCR pass, and nothing ever released it. The fix is the CFData variant plus an explicit autorelease pool around every Vision request. On the same route image, the repaired path holds steady at 178–180 MB across OCR passes 20 through 60.
A leak this size is invisible for the first twenty minutes. Anything meant to run unattended has to be measured over the duration it will actually run, not the duration you have patience for.

blocks.text: A shell-script bundle cannot hold a permission

blocks.html: The first version of the menu-bar app was an application bundle whose executable was a small script that exec'd Python. It launched, the menu appeared, everything looked right, and every permission stayed unchecked no matter how many times I granted it in System Settings.

exec replaces the process. So the thing macOS sees asking for Screen Recording is the Python framework binary, not the application. The identity the user granted and the identity making the request are two different programs. A bundle has to contain the executable that actually runs.
Diagnosed from a log file, because py2app sends stdout to the unified log where nobody looks. The app now writes to~/Library/Logs/ whenever it isn't attached to a terminal.

blocks.text: Ad-hoc signatures are derived from content

blocks.html: macOS ties permission grants to an application's code signature. An ad-hoc signature puts content hashes into the designated requirement, which means every rebuild is a different application as far as the permission database is concerned. Grant Screen Recording, change one line, rebuild, and the grant is silently gone.

That failure is worse than it sounds, because the macro does not crash without Screen Recording. It runs perfectly and sees a blank frame. The fix is a self-signed certificate, so the requirement depends on the bundle identifier and the certificate instead of the file contents. I verified it by rebuilding after a real change to a source file and diffing the requirement: byte-identical.

The build script creates that certificate itself. Two things about it look like problems and are not: the identity reports as untrusted, and signing works anyway, because trust governs verification of downloaded applications and this one is never distributed.

sections.h: The failure that doesn't raise an error

blocks.html: Without Screen Recording, macOS does not return an error. It returns a blank frame. The macro then runs happily, reads nothing, decides nothing, and clicks nowhere, which from the outside is indistinguishable from a bug in the vision code you are about to spend an evening not finding.

blocks.alt: The av-mac menu bar panel, showing a stopped state, a note that Roblox is not running, Start, Session, Settings, and permission rows for Screen Recording and Accessibility, both checked.
blocks.label: Plate 02
blocks.cap: The permission rows are clickable on purpose. Opening the System Settings pane by hand is not enough: an application that has never requested a permission is not listed there at all, so the row has to make the request itself.

blocks.html: There is an API that is supposed to tell you whether you have the permission. On this machine it returns false while capture works perfectly. So nothing asks; everything checks behaviourally. The diagnostic command walks the whole chain (interpreter, packages, both permissions, the window, capture, OCR, classification), and the capture step inspects the pixel range of the frame it just took. A frame with no range is the blank-frame failure, and it gets reported by name instead of showing up as a mystery.
The diagnostic sends no input at all, which is what makes it usable. You can run it any time, including while trying to work out whether the thing is broken or the game just changed.
An automation loop that guesses is worse than one that stops. Most of the design decisions here are about narrowing what the macro is willing to do when it is unsure.
A screen the classifier cannot name is written to disk as a PNG and its OCR dump, and nothing is clicked. Every new one is a bug report with the evidence already attached.
A floor number only updates after two consecutive consistent readings. A single misread used to latch permanently and re-trigger a restart on every later poll.
Recovery attempts are counted, not retried forever. After three failed attempts to close a stuck menu the runner exits rather than clicking into a state it does not understand.
Three independent stops that don't depend on the loop being healthy: the pointer in any screen corner, the game losing focus, and a hard cap on total actions.

The tests are written against the same principle. They pin the reasoning rather than the behaviour, and every test that exists because of a real bug is named after the bug, so the diff that breaks one tells you which mistake you are about to repeat.

items: test_single_floor_misread_cannot_latchOne bad reading used to stick permanently and re-trigger a restart forever.
test_restart_does_not_thrashThe restart trigger disarms after firing and only re-arms on a confirmed lower floor.
test_impossible_wave_maxima_are_droppedThe game's outlined 5 reads as a 3. A maximum below the current value is dropped, not believed.

sections.h: What is verified, and what isn't

blocks.html: Reading and deciding are verified thoroughly, because recorded captures make that cheap. Acting is verified much less, because every check costs a real run. Both lists are below, and the second one is longer.

items: All 79 captures classify correctly. Zero unknown.
A destination picked on 16 of 16 real atlas captures.
Floor number read on 45 of 47 in-match frames, range 1–18.
The full cash-out sequence landed on a live run, three clicks deep.
The installed application drove a real run and routed two floors.
The card handler has never actually clicked a card. Its offset is reasoned from one screenshot, not measured.
Three screen handlers may belong to an older game mode that no longer exists. Kept as safety nets, not claimed as features.
The treasure exclusion has only been proven against recorded captures; no live atlas has offered one yet.
Everything is measured on one machine, one macOS version, one window size.

blocks.html: So when I say it should work at other window sizes, that's reasoning, not a test result.

Automating a Roblox game violates Roblox's Terms of Service. An account running this can get banned, and clicking on a regular cadence for hours is exactly the pattern enforcement looks for. Nothing here is designed to be undetectable, and nothing here should be treated as though it were.

I'm publishing it anyway, with the warning at the top of the repository. The parts worth reading (window capture, OCR-driven state modeling, colour classification, the macOS permission model, and keeping track of what you tested versus what you assumed) work the same whether the window belongs to a game or to anything else.

There is a smaller commitment in it too. The recorded captures ship with the account name painted out, and the repository says to check your screenshots before attaching them to an issue. A debugging tool that collects screenshots is a tool that collects whatever was on screen.

The whole capture, OCR, and input stack is macOS frameworks, so it only runs on a Mac. Unit placement isn't automated, because the game's own automation handles it and a per-map coordinate database would be a lot of work for a mode that doesn't need it. And a game update that changes wording or layout will break screen detection. That is the expected failure mode, which is why the fix path is one file of rules and a set of captures that can be re-classified in a few seconds.
I'm a senior at Allen High School, in the IB Diploma Programme, graduating in 2027. Most of my time outside class goes into building things and teaching people how to build things.

What I keep coming back to is the seam between software and something physical or consequential. A model that classifies images is a contained problem. A model that has to identify robots in shaky phone footage from row 20, so a strategy team can decide who to pick, is a different one. When it's wrong, a team picks the wrong partner, and most of the interesting work ends up happening around the model, not inside it.

That's roughly the shape of everything on this site. On the scouting platform, the hard part turned out to be knowing which outputs you can trust. Most of the engineering in the hardening framework went into not breaking the machine. The cryptography course ends on a release decision instead of a definitions quiz. And at Eaglets I don't design the kits, I run the camps, which means the constraint I'm working against is a nine-year-old with forty minutes and an adult who has never seen a breadboard.

The research side is the other half, and it runs on the same instinct. I began my extended essay in 2025. It asks how far Itô calculus gets you when solving stochastic differential equations, and where each kind of exact answer runs out. My physics investigation measured whether a warm capacitor discharges differently than a cold one, and the data came back disagreeing with my hypothesis, which was the most useful thing about it.

A lot of what I do is teaching, and I didn't plan that. I've taught Java and object-oriented programming, Python and C++ and robotics at camps, programming fundamentals to kids, and now a cryptography course for adults.

It has made me a better engineer. You can't teach something you only understand well enough to use. Trying to explain why a certain design is right to someone who has no reason to take your word for it exposes the parts you were taking on faith fast.

Research programs, internships, and collaborations where I'd be working on real systems with people who know more than I do. I'm most interested in machine learning applied to physical systems, computer vision, security, and mathematical modeling, but I care more about the problem being real than about which of those boxes it falls into.

rows: IB Extended Essay · Mathematics · Started 2025 · 4,000 words

head.html: To what extent does Itô calculus enable analytical solutions of one-dimensional stochastic differential equations arising from standard Brownian motion?

The starting observation is that "solvable" isn't one thing. A model might give you an explicit formula for the path, or a known distribution at a fixed time, or closed expressions for moments, without giving you all three. Itô calculus applies to all four models in the paper. What varies is how much exactness you get out of it.

The setup is standard. A Wiener process Wt is the formal model of Brownian motion: continuous everywhere, differentiable nowhere, which is why ordinary calculus can't handle it. A one-dimensional Itô process is written
dXt = a(Xt, t)dt + b(Xt, t)dWt(1)
where a is the drift and b the diffusion. Itô's formula is the chain rule for such a process, and it carries a second-order term that ordinary calculus has no reason to keep. For a smooth f(Xt, t),
df = (∂f∂t + a∂f∂x +12b2∂2f∂x2) dt + b∂f∂xdWt(2)
That ½ b2 ∂2f/∂x2 term is the whole difference. It exists because (dW)2 =dt, which is not something a smooth function ever does.

It's worth pausing on, because it's why stochastic calculus looks so different from the calculus everyone learns first. Subdivide a Brownian path and add up the squared increments: the sum doesn't vanish the way it would for a smooth curve. It converges to the elapsed time. Try it below.
I picked the four models so that each one changes exactly one structural feature, which turns the survey into something closer to a controlled experiment.
Geometric Brownian motion
Multiplicative diffusion. Becomes additive under log St.
Ornstein–Uhlenbeck
Linear drift, constant diffusion. Gaussian at every fixed time.
Cox–Ingersoll–Ross
Square-root diffusion, with a boundary at 0.
Stochastic logistic
Nonlinear quadratic drift with multiplicative diffusion.

The result is a gradient, not a clean dividing line. GBM and OU satisfy all three criteria, giving explicit path formulas, recognizable finite-time distributions, and closed expressions for moments. CIR loses the elementary path formula but keeps an exact transition law, a noncentral chi-square, precisely because of its square-root diffusion and its behavior near zero. The logistic model has an explicit pathwise solution after a reciprocal transformation, yet its dependence on an exponential Brownian integral blocks a comparably simple finite-time distribution.
So drift, diffusion, and boundary behavior between them determine which kind of exact result you can have, to a large but limited extent. That's the argument.

The claim, laid out. Two things decide whether an exact solution exists: what the drift depends on, and what the diffusion depends on. Nonlinear drift turns out to be survivable. Nonlinear diffusion is where it stops.
The same four processes, simulated. Each is integrated with the same scheme over the same interval, so what you see is the structure of the model rather than an artifact of the method.

head.s: What Euler–Maruyama is doing, and why it's not free

blocks.html: It's the direct analogue of Euler's method: step forward with the drift, then add a random increment scaled by the square root of the step. The square root matters. Brownian increments scale with √dt, not dt, which is the numerical shadow of the same fact that makes Itô's formula need a second-order term.

It's also only order 1/2 in the strong sense, so halving the step doesn't halve the error the way it would for a deterministic solver. The naive scheme also doesn't respect a process's domain. A CIR path can be pushed negative by a large increment even though the true process can't go there, which is why the simulation above clamps it. The gap between the equation and what a solver does to it is part of what the paper is about.

head.s: Why volatility scaling with the state changes the problem

blocks.html: In geometric Brownian motion the diffusion term carries the state, so a path near zero moves in small absolute steps and a path high up moves in large ones. That's what keeps it positive and makes the log-transform work. Take logs and Itô's formula turns a multiplicative process into an additive one with constant coefficients.
That trick is available because the state appears linearly. The nonlinear model is constructed so no such substitution exists, which is exactly the property being tested.

blocks.html: Neither of these is separate from the engineering. The physics investigation came straight out of managing the electrical system on the robot. I wanted to know whether warm components behave differently in a way I could actually measure. They do, by 21%.

The extended essay connects less directly. Ratings in FRCMOB are an estimation problem under uncertainty: you're inferring a team's strength from a small, noisy, unevenly distributed sample, and any answer worth giving comes with a measure of how sure you are. Asking how far exact analysis will take you before you have to simulate is the same question as asking how much a rating built on four matches is really telling you.

Both also taught me the same thing about evidence. The physics data contradicted my hypothesis, and the right move was to report that rather than round it toward the prediction. That's the same discipline behind holding out an event to benchmark a detector.

head.html: How does the temperature of an electrolytic capacitor affect its effective discharge time constant, τ, in an RC circuit?

This one came directly out of robotics. Part of what I did at competition was manage the battery and electrical system, and components that have been running for a while are warm. I wanted to know whether that changes their behavior in a way you could measure.
An ideal capacitor discharging through a resistor decays exponentially,
V(t) = V0e−t/τ, τ = RC(3)

Real electrolytic capacitors leak. Imperfections in the aluminium oxide dielectric let a small current through, and that leakage rises with temperature as charge carriers pick up thermal energy. The leakage acts like a resistance in parallel with the capacitor, which lowers the effective resistance and shortens τ.
I measured discharge curves at five temperatures from 10 °C to 50 °C through a fixed 47 kΩ resistor. Taking logs linearizes the decay,
ln V(t) =ln V0 −tτ(4)

so a plot of ln V against t is a straight line of gradient m = −1/τ, and τ = −1/m falls straight out of the regression. I linearized instead of curve-fitting so that any departure from exponential behavior would show up as visible curvature, not hide inside a fit.
−21% over 40 °C

τ fell monotonically across the range, and the step between adjacent temperatures was about six times the measurement uncertainty, so the effect isn't noise. Every linearized fit had R² above 0.9995, which also confirms the discharge stayed single-exponential throughout.

The part I find more interesting is where it disagreed with me. I predicted an Arrhenius-type response: since dielectric conductivity depends exponentially on temperature, each successive 10 °C step should have produced a progressively larger drop in τ. It didn't. The steps came out near-uniform, and a straight line fits the whole 40 °C range,
Over this span the response is linear, and the exponential curvature the mechanism predicts doesn't show up in the data at all.

head.s: Uncertainty, and why I didn't just use a trendline

blocks.html: Rather than take a single regression gradient at face value, I wrote the analysis in Python and searched for the extreme gradients still consistent with every point's error bar: the steepest and shallowest lines that stay feasible given ±0.01 V on each reading. That gives a real bound on the gradient, instead of reporting a fit statistic as though it were an uncertainty.
The uncertainty in τ then follows from the reciprocal relationship,
Δτ = τ2 Δm
which is what puts the ±0.4 s on each value above.

rows: RC discharge at 10–50 °C · fixed 47 kΩ resistor · log-linearization · gradient-bounded uncertainty analysis in Python

vision-pipeline.title: Film
vision-pipeline.detail: The scout films the match from the stands, or uploads a clip they already have. Everything after this happens on the phone; the video never has to reach a server.

vision-pipeline.title: Calibrate
vision-pipeline.detail: Four taps on the field corners give the image-to-field correspondences, and a homography is fit from them. The calibration frame is stored, and the first recording frame is registered against it, so a phone that moved gets asked to re-calibrate instead of producing quietly wrong positions.
vision-pipeline.note: AprilTags were the original plan. From the stands they're too small to decode, so taps became the main path.

vision-pipeline.title: Detect
vision-pipeline.detail: Detector v4 runs in the browser through ONNX Runtime Web. It reads only the calibrated field area, not the whole frame. Devices with a GPU get the full model on WebGPU; the rest get a nano model on multithreaded WebAssembly.
vision-pipeline.note: v4 at a 0.35 cutoff on WebGPU, v4-nano at 0.25 on WASM. Holdout mAP@50 77.9% and 74.0%.

vision-pipeline.title: Track
vision-pipeline.detail: Detections are associated in field coordinates rather than pixels, with a speed limit a real robot can't beat, so a camera pan doesn't break a path. Fragments are then stitched conservatively: two pieces join only when the robot reappears soon, close by, and in its own alliance's colour.
vision-pipeline.note: Stitching rule: reappears within 2 s, within 0.5 m + 2 m/s of where it vanished.

vision-pipeline.title: Identify
vision-pipeline.detail: The scout taps once per robot to say which team it is, helped by each team's robot photo and by suggestions that continue a path from where an identified robot was last seen. Suggestions are marked as suggestions; about one in ten is wrong, and the screen says so.

vision-pipeline.title: Summarize
vision-pipeline.detail: Identified paths become heat maps, zone time, and an attack-versus-defense split. Accepted runs feed Team Center and the auto-scout drafts that a human reviews.

avmac-pipeline.title: Capture the window
avmac-pipeline.detail: CGWindowListCreateImage reads the target window's own backing store, so whatever is stacked on top of it never lands in the frame. Roughly 33 ms per frame, and the application can sit behind other windows the whole time.
avmac-pipeline.note: A screen-rectangle grab measured 31 ms and returned the wrong pixels whenever anything overlapped.

avmac-pipeline.title: Read the text
avmac-pipeline.detail: Apple's Vision framework returns strings with positions. Everything is located by what it says rather than by matching stored images, which means a window resize or a reskin that keeps the wording does not break it.
avmac-pipeline.note: Accurate recognition level, with language correction off, because the strings are unit names, not English.

avmac-pipeline.title: Classify the screen
avmac-pipeline.detail: A rule set turns a bag of strings into one answer: which screen is this. Fuzzy token matching, not set equality, because OCR reads the same frame slightly differently every time.
avmac-pipeline.note: state.classify: the rules live in one file, so a game update has one place to fix.

avmac-pipeline.title: Decide
avmac-pipeline.detail: One handler per screen. Handlers are pure decisions over a parsed frame, which is why the whole decision layer is testable against recorded captures with no game running and no permissions granted.
avmac-pipeline.note: An unrecognized screen is written to disk, never clicked at.

avmac-pipeline.title: Act, then look again
avmac-pipeline.detail: CGEventPost synthesizes the click. Nothing is fire-and-forget: the next frame has to confirm the click registered, because a click that silently did nothing is the failure mode that strands a long run.
avmac-pipeline.note: Corner abort, focus-loss abort, and a hard action cap all stop it from outside.
